title: Vault Account
statement: Model a simple savings vault as an object with three methods. deposit(amount) adds money. withdraw(amount) removes money only if the balance covers it, reporting true on success and false (with no change) otherwise. balance() reports the current balance. The vault starts at 0. Given a list of calls such as ["deposit", 50], ["withdraw", 20] or ["balance"], apply them in order and return the results of every withdraw and balance call, in order. Deposits produce no result.

examples.explanation: Withdrawing 20 succeeds (30 left); withdrawing 40 fails, so the balance stays 30.

hints.content: Treat this as a class with one private field: the current balance.
deposit and balance are one-line methods.
withdraw has to check before it changes anything.
Only withdraw and balance produce results, so push to the results list only for those calls.
Recomputing the balance from a history of transactions works, but a single running total makes every call O(1).

testCases.explanation: Withdrawing 20 succeeds (30 left); withdrawing 40 fails, so the balance stays 30.
Withdrawing from an empty vault fails.
Withdrawing the exact balance succeeds and leaves 0.
Balances can exceed the per-call limit: 3000000, then 2000000 after withdrawing the maximum amount.
A failed withdrawal leaves the balance unchanged for the next call.

solutions.title: Recompute from the transaction history
solutions.intuition: The balance is the sum of every successful transaction, so keep the history and add it up when needed.
solutions.approach: Store each successful deposit as +amount and each successful withdrawal as -amount. For withdraw and balance, sum the history first.
solutions.pseudocode:
history = []
for op: deposit → history.push(+a); withdraw → ok = sum(history) >= a; if ok: history.push(-a); out.push(ok); balance → out.push(sum(history))
commonMistakes: Recording failed withdrawals in the history.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Replaying the history is how an audit log works and is clearly correct, but each query costs O(history), so it's quadratic overall.

solutions.title: Encapsulated running balance
solutions.intuition: The only state that affects future calls is the current balance.
solutions.approach: Write a small Vault class with a private balance and deposit, withdraw and balance methods, then dispatch each operation to it.
solutions.pseudocode: class Vault: balance = 0; deposit(a): balance += a; withdraw(a): if a > balance: return false; balance -= a; return true; read(): return balance
commonMistakes: Letting callers modify the balance directly instead of through methods.
Subtracting first and checking for a negative balance afterwards, which briefly breaks the invariant.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I'd model this as a class whose private field is the balance, with the invariant that it's never negative. withdraw checks before mutating, so a failed call has no side effects. Every call is O(1). In a real system I'd use integer cents to avoid floating-point error, and I'd keep an append-only transaction log alongside the running total for auditing.
